{{Short description|Property of structural isomorphism}}
In [[mathematics]], particularly in [[universal algebra]] and [[category theory]], '''transport of structure''' refers to the process whereby a [[mathematical object]] acquires a new [[mathematical structure|structure]] and its [[Canonical form|canonical definitions]], as a result of being [[isomorphic]] to (or otherwise identified with) another object with a pre-existing structure.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Holm|first=Henrik|date=2015|title=A Note on Transport of Algebraic Structures|url=http://www.tac.mta.ca/tac/volumes/30/34/30-34.pdf|journal=Theory and Applications of Categories|volume=30|issue=34|pages=1121–1131|arxiv=1504.07366}}</ref> Definitions by transport of structure are regarded as canonical.

==Examples==
Since mathematical structures are often defined in reference to an underlying [[space (mathematics)|space]], many examples of transport of structure involve spaces and [[Map (mathematics)|mappings]] between them.  For example, if ''<math>V</math>'' and ''<math>W</math>'' are [[vector space]]s with <math>(\cdot,\cdot)</math> being an [[inner product]] on <math>W</math>, such that there is an [[isomorphism]] <math>\phi</math> from ''<math>V</math>'' to ''<math>W</math>'', then one can define an inner product <math>[\cdot, \cdot]</math> on ''<math>V</math>'' by the following rule:

:<math>[v_1, v_2] = (\phi(v_1), \phi(v_2))</math>

Although the equation makes sense even when <math>\phi</math> is not an isomorphism, it only defines an inner product on ''<math>V</math>'' when <math>\phi</math> is, since otherwise it will cause <math>[\cdot,\cdot]</math> to be [[degenerate bilinear form|degenerate]].  The idea is that <math>\phi</math> allows one to consider ''<math>V</math>'' and ''<math>W</math>'' as "the same" vector space, and by following this analogy, then one can transport an inner product from one space to the other.

A more elaborated example comes from [[differential topology]], in which the notion of [[smooth manifold]] is involved: if <math>M</math> is such a manifold, and if ''<math>X</math>'' is any [[topological space]] which is [[homeomorphic]] to ''<math>M</math>'', then one can consider ''<math>X</math>'' as a smooth manifold as well. That is, given a homeomorphism <math>\phi \colon X \to M</math>, one can define coordinate charts on ''<math>X</math>'' by "pulling back" coordinate charts on ''<math>M</math>'' through <math>\phi</math>.  Recall that a coordinate chart on <math>M</math> is an [[open set]] ''<math>U</math>'' together with an [[injective]] map
:<math>c \colon U \to \mathbb{R}^n</math>

for some [[natural number]] ''<math>n</math>''; to get such a chart on ''<math>X</math>'', one uses the following rules:

:<math>U' = \phi^{-1}(U)</math> and <math>c' = c \circ \phi</math>.

Furthermore, it is required that the charts [[Cover (topology)|cover]] ''<math>M</math>'' (the fact that the transported charts cover ''<math>X</math>'' follows immediately from the fact that <math>\phi</math> is a [[bijection]]). Since ''<math>M</math>'' is a ''smooth'' manifold, if ''U'' and ''V'', with their maps <math>c \colon U \to \mathbb{R}^n</math> and <math>d \colon V \to \mathbb{R}^n</math>, are two charts on ''<math>M</math>'', then the composition, the "transition map"

:<math>d \circ c^{-1} \colon c(U \cap V) \to \mathbb{R}^n</math> (a self-map of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>)

is smooth. To verify this for the transported charts on ''<math>X</math>'', notice that

:<math>\phi^{-1}(U) \cap \phi^{-1}(V) = \phi^{-1}(U \cap V)</math>,
and therefore
:<math>c'(U' \cap V') = (c \circ \phi)(\phi^{-1}(U \cap V)) = c(U \cap V)</math>, and
:<math>d' \circ (c')^{-1} = (d \circ \phi) \circ (c \circ \phi)^{-1} = d \circ (\phi \circ \phi^{-1}) \circ c^{-1} = d \circ c^{-1}</math>.

Thus the transition map for <math>U'</math> and <math>V'</math> is the same as that for ''<math>U</math>'' and ''<math>V</math>'', hence smooth.  That is, ''<math>X</math>'' is a smooth manifold via transport of structure. This is a special case of transport of structures in general.<ref>{{Citation
 | last = Bourbaki
 | first = Nicolas
 | author-link=Nicolas Bourbaki
 | title = Elements of mathematics: Theory of sets
 | year = 1968
 | publisher = Hermann (original), Addison-Wesley (translation)
}}, Chapter IV, Section 5 "Isomorphism and transport of structures".</ref>

The second example also illustrates why "transport of structure" is not always desirable. Namely, one can take ''<math>M</math>'' to be the plane, and ''<math>X</math>'' to be an infinite one-sided cone.  By "flattening" the cone, a homeomorphism of ''<math>X</math>'' and ''<math>M</math>'' can be obtained, and therefore the structure of a smooth manifold on ''<math>X</math>'', but the cone is not "naturally" a smooth manifold. That is, one can consider ''<math>X</math>'' as a subspace of 3-space, in which context it is not smooth at the cone point.  

A more surprising example is that of [[exotic sphere]]s, discovered by [[John Milnor]], which states that there are exactly 28 smooth manifolds which are [[homeomorphic]] but ''not'' [[diffeomorphic]] to <math>S^7</math>, the 7-dimensional sphere in 8-space. Thus, transport of structure is most productive when there exists a [[canonical form|canonical]] isomorphism between the two objects.
